paras: The threatened lynching of James Bradford took place on the night of August 6, 1910, when a crowd gathered outside the Culver building in downtown St. Louis, Missouri, shouting for the lynching of Bradford, a Black janitor whom police had just arrested on the accusation of luring a young white woman, Bessie Unger, to his room with a false job advertisement. Police removed Bradford from the crowd, and he was later bound over to a grand jury on two charges. Dispatches about the case ran in white papers across the country, several under headlines that linked it to lynching.

Bradford, who gave his age as 47, was janitor of the Culver building at 306 North Twelfth Street. A newspaper advertisement asked for a neat young woman between 20 and 25, a high school graduate, to work as an office assistant at good wages. According to the wire dispatch, Bessie Smith answered it on Thursday and gave her telephone number, and when a call came that night her father, J. B. Smith, grew suspicious, after which police arranged an "ambuscade" for Saturday night.

Unger, 22, answered the advertisement and went to the building on the night of August 6. Led by a woman's scream, Sergeant Wade Matthews and three patrolmen forced the locked door of the janitor's room. The Keokuk Daily Gate City's version said they found Unger on her knees "begging for mercy" while Bradford threatened her with a revolver, and that she had bruises where he had choked her. Other dispatches said Bradford flourished a revolver and threatened the officers with death, and police later asserted that he had tried to shoot Matthews.

A crowd soon gathered at Twelfth and Olive streets, crying "lynch him" and "lynch the brute," and the police had difficulty keeping Bradford from it. The Gate City said he was "spirited away" to police headquarters, while the United Press reported that a mob threatened to lynch him on the spot and that he was put in jail only with difficulty. Police said his pockets held answers to the advertisement from young women and the photographs of five white girls.

On August 8 Matthews and Unger applied for a warrant, and the police based a charge of attempted criminal assault on the locked door and the alleged attempt to shoot the sergeant. Detective Cooper, a Black officer, identified Bradford as James Bradfield, who had been fined $50 on each of four counts in 1908 after two white women said he tried to drag them into a room, fines that were stayed when white persons intervened for him. Bradford told reporters he never intended to harm any of the girls and said he had a white wife whom he had married in Illinois.

The same day a second woman, Lulu Fehlhammer, told police that Bradford had held a pistol to her head the previous week and made her sign a statement that she had come of her own free will, a statement police said they found among his effects with a lock of her hair. By August 16 Chief of Police Young was examining a love letter signed "Dr. Merrell" that police believed Bradford had written to another young woman who had answered the advertisements, though she denied receiving it. On August 20, after Unger testified, Judge Klone of the criminal correction court held Bradford under $5,000 bail on two charges and bound him over to the grand jury. No report of the grand jury's action, a trial, or any arrest of members of the crowd appears in the coverage.

The case reached readers through at least two wire versions on August 7 and 8, and every account found came from white papers, from Montgomery and Shreveport to Omaha, Tacoma and Los Angeles. The Keokuk Daily Gate City put the story on its front page under the headline "Why Lynching Is So Popular," presenting the accusation as an explanation for lynching. The Albuquerque Morning Journal headed the dispatch "Narrowly Escapes Lynching When Captured," the Tacoma Times ran the United Press version as "Threaten to Lynch Negro," and the Montgomery Advertiser and the Shreveport Caucasian used "Girl Saved From Negro" and "Decoyed by Negro."

The dispatches called Bradford "the negro" or "the black," stressed the photographs of white girls in his pockets, and gave the police version as fact. Only the East St. Louis Daily Journal printed Bradford's own words, under the headline "Negro Has a White Wife." Follow-up stories on the second complainant and the love letter ran as far away as Montana and California, and no Black newspaper account was found.

Accounts of the arrest differ: the Gate City said Bradford fled down a corridor and fell 20 feet from a window into an alley, the wire dispatch said he was locked up after a struggle, and the East St. Louis paper said Matthews knocked him from a second-story window. Reports also give his name as Bradford or Bradfield and place the Fehlhammer attack on a Tuesday or a Wednesday. All versions of the accusations against him came from the police and the complainants.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of James Bradford
bases: The episode is a crowd's cries to lynch a Black man as police arrested him, with no attack on him reported (A1, A3, A10); it is a threatened lynching, coded under lynching at the threatened stage.

A crowd shouted 'lynch him' and 'lynch the brute' over an accused assault on a white woman, but police removed Bradford and he was not killed (A1, A3, A10); he was later bound over to a grand jury (A26).

The Keokuk dispatch, the leased-wire dispatch in Montgomery and Albuquerque, the United Press report and the East St. Louis paper agree on the arrest at the Culver building and the crowd's cries to lynch him (A1, A3, A4, A9, A10).

accounts.label: Keokuk dispatch
accounts.gist: Police broke down the door, found Unger on her knees as Bradford threatened her with a revolver; he fled and fell 20 feet into an alley; a great crowd cried 'lynch him' but he was spirited away.

accounts.label: Leased-wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Police guided by J. B. Smith rescued Unger; Bradford flourished a revolver and threatened the officers and was locked up after a struggle; a crowd shouting 'lynch the brute' gathered and police had difficulty saving him.

accounts.label: United Press
accounts.gist: A policeman rescued Unger; a mob threatened to lynch Bradford on the spot and he was placed in jail with difficulty.

accounts.label: Police (East St. Louis report)
accounts.gist: Police based an attempted-assault charge on the locked door and an alleged attempt to shoot Sgt. Matthews, who knocked Bradford from a second-story window.

accounts.label: Bradford
accounts.gist: He said he never intended to harm any of the white girls and that he had a white wife he married in Illinois.

framing.detail: The Keokuk Daily Gate City headed the story 'Why Lynching Is So Popular', presenting the accusation as an explanation for lynching.
Wire versions ran as 'Girl Saved From Negro', 'Narrowly Escapes Lynching When Captured', 'Threaten to Lynch Negro' and 'Decoyed by Negro', in the police's account.
The East St. Louis Daily Journal printed Bradford's denial under 'Negro Has a White Wife', alongside his prior arrest record.
